Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 57, verse 7–8:

*Mustakhlafina fihi* (appointed as successors regarding it): the meaning is that the wealth that is in your hands is in reality the wealth of Allah, by His creating and originating it. He is the one who gave you wealth, granted you the enjoyment of it, and made you successors in disposing of it. So it is not truly your own wealth. You are in it only in the position of agents and deputies. So spend from it in the rights of Allah, and let spending from it be easy for you, just as spending from another man's property is easy for a person when that man has permitted him to do so. Or (the meaning is) that He made you successors of those who came before you in what is in your hands, by bequeathing it to you. So take warning from their condition, since it passed from them to you, and it will pass from you to those after you. Therefore do not be stingy with it, and benefit yourselves by spending from it.

*Wa-ma lakum la tu'minuna* (And what is wrong with you that you do not believe): *la tu'minuna* is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the sense of the verb in *mal-akum* (what is wrong with you), as you say: *ma-lak qa'iman* (what is wrong with you standing), meaning: what are you doing standing; that is: *wa-ma lakum kafirina billah* (and what is wrong with you, being disbelievers in Allah). The *wa* in *wa-l-Rasulu yad'ukum* (while the Messenger calls you) is the *wa* of circumstance, so the two are interlocking circumstantial clauses. It has also been read:

*Wa-ma lakum la tu'minuna billahi wa-r-Rasulu yad'ukum* (And what is wrong with you that you do not believe in Allah, while the Messenger calls you). The meaning is: what excuse do you have for abandoning faith, when the Messenger calls you to it, admonishes you about it, and recites to you the Book, which speaks with clear proofs and arguments? Moreover, Allah has already taken your covenant to believe, by setting intellects within you [[Mahmud said: "Taking the covenant is an expression for the composition of intellects in them... etc." Ahmad said: There is nothing wrong in taking the covenant to be understood as Allah explained it in another verse, since He, the Exalted, says: "And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes.'" But what troubles me about him is his denial of many such outward expressions and his turning them away from their realities, although they are rationally possible and certainly established by revelation, toward what he imagines to be a figurative representation that he calls imagination. The rule you should rely on, so that it does not harm you, is that not everything which reason permits and which revelation has reported as occurring must be taken in its outward sense. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] and by appointing proofs for you, enabling you to reflect, and removing your excuses. Surah 57, verse 12: "On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and by their right hands..."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf):

"Yawma tara" (On the Day you see) is an adverbial complement (zarf) governing His saying: "and for them is a noble reward." Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, "remember" (udhkur), to magnify that Day.

As for His saying "before them and by their right hands," it is because the blessed (al-su'ada') are given the records of their deeds from these two directions, just as the wretched (al-ashqiya') are given them from their left hands and from behind their backs. So He made the light in both directions a sign and emblem for them, because they are the ones who were made happy by their good deeds and who prospered through their white records. When they are taken to Paradise and pass over the Sirat, "running" (yas'a): the light runs with their running, going before them and leading them on.

And those angels who receive them say to them: "Good tidings for you today!" It is also read: "dhalika al-fawz" (that is the triumph).

On the Day when the hypocrite men and women will say to those who believed: "Wait for us (unzurūnā), that we may borrow of your light." It is said: the phrase is a substitute (badal) for "a Day you will see" (in the previous verse, 57:12).

"Unzurūnā" means "intaẓirūnā," "wait for us," because they are hurried toward Paradise like swift lightning flashes, upon mounts (rikāb) that carry them swiftly (tazuff bihim), i.e., hasten them (the commentary on this phrase: "tazuff bihim" means "they hasten," as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ). And these (the hypocrites) are on foot. "And look at us" (unzurū ilaynā), because when they look toward them, they face them with their faces, and the light is before them, so they are illuminated by it.

It was also read "anẓirūnā," from the "naẓra," which is respite (al-imhāl). The hastening of their pace in going on until they reach them is made a respite for them: "that we may borrow of your light," the verb being in the subjunctive after "min" (in the sense of "from"), and that is that they reach them and be illuminated by it.

"It will be said: Return behind you, and seek light." This is a rebuke and mockery of them; i.e., return to the place of standing (al-mawqif), to where this light was given, and seek it there; thence one borrows it. Or: return to the world and seek light by acquiring its cause, which is faith. Or: return disappointed and withdraw from us, and seek another light; you have no way to this light. They knew that there was no light behind them; it was only a means of disappointment and despair for them.

"So a wall will be set up between them, with a gate (bāb) in it." A barrier, a wall intervening between the two sides, Paradise and Hell. It is said: the wall is al-A'rāf. For that wall there is a gate for the people of Paradise, through which they enter. "Its inside (bāṭinuhu) is mercy, and its outside (ẓāhiruhu) is from before it torment." Its inside, i.e., the inside of the wall or of the gate, is the side that is toward Paradise; and its outside is what appears to the people of Hell from its side, from its direction: the torment, which is darkness and fire.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them both) read: "fa-ḍuriba baynahum" in the active voice (fa-ḍaraba). "Did we not used to be with you?" They mean agreement with them outwardly. "They say: Yes, but you tempted yourselves (fatantum anfusakum), afflicted them with hypocrisy and destroyed them, and you waited for the believers to fall into misfortunes, and deceiving desires (al-amānī) deluded you — long hopes and greed for the prolonging of life — until the command of Allah came, which is death. And the Deceiver (al-Gharūr) deceived you about Allah," i.e., Satan deceived you by saying that Allah is Forgiving and Generous and will not punish you. It was also read "al-Ghurūr" with a dammah.

"Today no ransom (fidyah) will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire (hiya mawlākum)." It is said: it is more deserving of you. And he recited the verse of Labīd:

*Fa-ghadat kilā al-farjayni taḥsabu annahu ... mawlā al-makhāfati khalfahā wa-amāmahā*

(This is from his Mu'allaqa. He describes a wild cow. "Tawajjasat": she listened intently; al-tawajjus is listening. It is said: "razzat al-samā' razzan" (with the rāʾ placed first) when it made a sound at the time of rain; al-razz with a fatḥah is a hidden sound, and with a kasrah it is the name for a hidden sound. "Razz al-anīs": the sound of the hunter, who frightened her from behind. Inserting "back" (ẓahr) in such a construction is for emphasis of concealment, because what is behind the back is not known. The hunter is called "anīs" in relation to us, not to her, because he is her torment and the cause of her fear; he is described as "the very sickness" (nafs al-saqām) as an intensification. "Kilā al-farjayn" is the subject; "taḥsabu annahu mawlā al-makhāfa" is the predicate, meaning that he is the most deserving of fear from her side. "Khalfahā wa-amāmahā" is a predicate of an omitted subject, or a substitute for "kilā al-farjayn" for clarification; i.e., for her are what is between her legs and what is before her hands. Some explained the two as two horns in the mountain, and on this reading there is no meaning for the definite article in them.)

Alam ya'ni (ألم يأن) is from anā al-amr ya'nī (أنى الأمر يأنى), meaning "when the matter came to its appointed time (inā'uhu), i.e., its time (waqtuhu)." It is also read ألم يئن (lam yi'n), from āna yā'īnu (آن يئين), with the same meaning as anā yaanī (أنى يأنى); and ألما يأن (alamma ya'n). It is said: they were in a state of drought in Makkah, and when they emigrated they attained provision and blessing, and so they became slack regarding what they had been upon, and this verse was revealed.

From Ibn Mas'ud: "Between our acceptance of Islam and the time when we were rebuked with this verse, there were only four years." [Narrated by Muslim with the wording "between the time when Allah rebuked us," and al-Hakim made an error and included it in his al-Mustadrak.]

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Allah was slow in the hearts of the believers, so He rebuked them at the thirteenth year after the revelation of the Qur'an began.

From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "By Allah, He was slow with them, while they were reciting less of the Qur'an than you recite. So consider the length of what you have recited of it, and what corruption has appeared among you."

From Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that this verse was recited in his presence, and with him were people from Yamamah, and they wept intensely. He looked at them and said: "This is how we were, until the hearts hardened."

It is read نزّل (nazzala) and نزل (nazala), and أنزل (anzala). وَلا يَكُونُوا (wa-la yakūnū, "and that they should not be") is a conjunction with تخشع (takhsha'a). It is read with the ta' (تكونوا... ) as an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). It is also permissible that it be a prohibition to them from imitating the People of the Book in hardness of hearts after they were rebuked. That is because the Children of Israel had the truth standing between them and their desires, and when they heard the Torah and the Gospel they humbled themselves to Allah and their hearts softened. But when time lengthened upon them, harshness and hardness overcame them, they differed, and they introduced what they introduced of distortion and other things.

If you say: What is the meaning of لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ (for the remembrance of Allah) and وَما نَزَلَ مِنَ الْحَقِّ (and what has been revealed of the truth)? I say: it is permissible that by the remembrance and by what has been revealed of the truth is meant the Qur'an, since it combines both aspects: it is a reminder and an admonition, and it is truth sent down from heaven. And it is permissible that what is meant is their humbling when Allah is remembered and when the Qur'an is recited, as in His saying: ﴿When Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾. By al-amad (الأمد) is meant the term (al-ajal), as in his saying: "... when its term (amad) has come to an end." (The full line is: "Every living thing completing the span of life... and everything that ends when its term (amad) is reached.")

[The explanatory note: the commentary on this line of verse was previously explained in the first volume, page 277, so consult it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]

It is read الأمدّ (al-amadd), meaning: the longer period. ﴿And many of them are defiant transgressors﴾: they are outside their religion, rejecting what is in the two Books.

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death.﴾ It has been said: this is an illustration (tamthil, a figurative likeness) of the effect of remembrance (dhikr) on hearts, and that He gives life to them just as the rain gives life to the earth.

Al-Mutaṣṣaddiqīn (ﷺ-less note): the form al-Mutaṣaddiqīn (those who give charity). It is also read according to the original form. Al-Muṣaddiqīn are from ṣaddaqa, and they are those who affirmed God and His Messenger, meaning the believers.

If you ask: on what is His saying "and have lent" (wa aqraḍū) coordinated? I say: it is coordinated on the meaning of the verb in al-muṣaddiqīn, because the lām is in the sense of alladhīna (those who), and the active participle is in the sense of "have affirmed," as if it were said: "Indeed those who have affirmed and lent."

The goodly loan (al-qarḍ al-ḥasan) is that one gives charity from good (wealth), out of a good soul and sound intention, to one who deserves the charity. It is also read yuḍʿafu and yuḍāʿifu with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra, meaning: God multiplies (it).

This passage is describing that the believers in Allah and His messengers are, in the sight of Allah, in the rank of the truthful (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs (al-shuhada'): they are those who hastened to affirm the truth and who were martyred in the way of Allah. "For them is their reward and their light" means: like the reward of the truthful and the martyrs, and like their light. If it is said: how can they be equated with them in reward when there must be a difference? The answer is: the meaning is that Allah gives the believers their reward and multiplies it for them by His bounty, so that their reward, together with its multiples, equals the reward of those others.

It is also permissible that "wa-al-shuhada'" (and the martyrs) be the subject (mubtada'), and "lahum ajruhum" (for them is their reward) be its predicate (khabar).

This is a commentary passage on Q. 57:20, so I'll translate it faithfully, transliterating technical terms with glosses on first occurrence and keeping the scholarly note as it stands.

He intends that the present world is nothing but trivial matters, namely play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in multiplying wealth and children.

As for the Hereafter, it is nothing but weighty matters, namely: severe punishment, forgiveness, and the good pleasure of Allah.

He likened the state of the world, its swift passing away together with its scant benefit, to a plant that the rain brought forth, so it grew and reached maturity (ikhtahala) [[His saying "fa-istawa wa-ktahal": in al-Sihah, "iktahala al-nabat" means its length became complete and its brightness appeared. (ʿA.)]]

The disbelievers who deny Allah's blessing in what He provided them of rain and plants are pleased with it. Then He sent a blight upon it, so it withered, turned yellow, and became debris (hutam), as a punishment for their ingratitude, just as He did to the people of the garden and the owner of the two gardens. It was said that al-kuffar (the disbelievers) means: the farmers (al-zurrāʿ). It is also read: muṣfāran (yellow).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 57, verse 21:

﴿Sābiqū﴾ (hasten): hurry eagerly, like racers competing with their peers on the course, ﴿to a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of the heaven and the earth﴾. Al-Suddi said: "Like the breadth of the seven heavens and the seven earths." The mention of breadth rather than length is because everything that has both breadth and length has a breadth less than its length; so when its breadth is described as expansive, it is understood that its length is even more expansive and extensive. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "breadth" is expansiveness, as in His saying: ﴿fa-dhū du'ā'in ʿarīḍ﴾ (one of abundant supplication). When He belittled the worldly life, reduced its matter, and magnified the matter of the Hereafter, He sent His servants to hasten toward attaining what He promised of that, namely the forgiveness that saves from severe punishment and the triumph of entering the Garden. ﴿That﴾ — the promised forgiveness and Garden — ﴿is the bounty of Allah﴾, His giving, ﴿which He bestows upon whom He wills﴾, and they are the believers.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 57, verses 22–24:

"Misfortune in the earth" means drought and blights affecting crops and fruit. "In yourselves" means ailments and death. ﴿Written in a Book, in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), before We bring it into being﴾: that is, the souls or the misfortunes. ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾: that is, its decree and its recording in the Book is easy for Allah, even if it is difficult for His servants. Then he gave the reason for this and explained its wisdom, saying: ﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you﴾. The meaning is that when you know that everything is predestined and written with Allah, your grief over what is lost and your joy over what is coming will be reduced. For whoever knows that what is with him is bound to end, his distress at losing it will not grow intense, because he has prepared himself for that. Likewise, whoever knows that some good will reach him, and that its arrival cannot be prevented in any way, his joy at attaining it will not be great. ﴿And Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾.

Because whoever rejoices in a portion of this world and is inflated within himself becomes conceited, boasts about it, and acts haughtily toward people.

It has been read as ﴿bi-mā ātākum﴾ and as ﴿atākum﴾, from (al-iytā') and (al-ityān) (both meaning "giving" or "bringing"). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿bi-mā ūtītum﴾. If you say: no one can keep himself from grief when harm befalls him, nor from joy when he obtains some benefit, so how can one avoid grief and joy altogether?

I say: what is meant is grief that drives a person to the point of losing patience, submission to Allah's command, and hope for the reward of the patient; and joy that becomes overbearing and distracts from gratitude. As for the grief that a person can hardly be free of while remaining submissive, and the happiness at Allah's blessing and taking account of it with gratitude, there is no harm in these.

﴿Those who are miserly﴾ is a substitution for ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾, as if He had said: "Allah does not love those who are miserly." He means those who rejoice with overbearing joy when they are given wealth and a portion of this world; because of their love for it, its esteem in their eyes, and its greatness in their sight, they withhold it from the rights of Allah and are stingy with it. It is not enough for them that they are miserly; they also compel people to be miserly, encourage them to hoard, and make it appealing to them. All of this is the result of their joy in it and their insolence when they obtain it.

﴿And whoever turns away﴾ from the commands and prohibitions of Allah, and does not refrain from what He has forbidden, namely grief over what is lost and joy over what is coming: then indeed Allah is ﴿Free of need﴾ of him.

It has been read as ﴿bi-l-bukhl﴾ (with stinginess). Nafi' read ﴿fa-inna Allāha al-Ghaniyy﴾, and it is written this way in the Qur'an codices of the people of Medina and Syria.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 57, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, We sent Our messengers with clear proofs,﴾ meaning the angels, to the prophets, [sent] with clear evidences (al-hujaj) and miracles (al-mu'jizat), ﴿and We sent down with them the Book﴾, i.e., the revelation (al-wahy), ﴿and the Balance﴾. It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with the balance, handed it to Nuh, and said: "Command your people to weigh with it."

﴿And We sent down iron﴾. It is said: Adam descended from the Garden, and with him were five items of iron: the anvil (al-sindan), the two tongs (al-kalabatan), the chisel (al-miqa'ah), the hammer (al-mitraqah), and the needle. It is also reported: and with him were the (al-marr) and the spade (al-misha). [[His words "wal-miqa'ah wal-mitraqah ... ila akhirihi": in al-Sihah, "al-miqa'ah" is the hammer. Al-miqa'ah also means a long whetstone. Al-marr is the rope, and al-misha is like the shovel (al-mijrafah), except that it is made of iron. (A)]]

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): that Allah, exalted is He, sent down four blessings from the heaven to the earth: He sent down iron, fire, water, and salt. [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and in its chain is someone I do not know.]]

And from al-Hasan: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ means: We created it, like His saying, ﴿And He sent down for you eight kinds of livestock﴾. That is because His commands descend from the heaven, along with His decrees and judgments. ﴿In it is great might﴾, namely, fighting with it; ﴿and benefits for mankind﴾ in their interests, livelihoods and crafts, for there is no craft in which iron is not an instrument, or [anything] that is worked with iron. ﴿That Allah may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen﴾, by using swords, spears, and all other weapons in striving against the enemies of the religion. ﴿Unseen﴾: absent from them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They help Him without seeing Him." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾: Self-sufficient through His power and might in destroying whomever He wills to destroy, without them. He only imposed jihad upon them so that they might benefit from it, and through obedience to the command concerning it, reach the reward.

And the Book and the revelation. From Ibn 'Abbas: writing with the pen. It is said: he wrote a book (kitab) and writing (kitaba). Among them, [that is,] among the descendants or among those to whom they were sent, and the mention of sending and of the messengers has indicated them. This is a detailed explanation of their condition, meaning: some of them are guided and some of them are defiant sinners, and the dominance is for the sinners.

Al-Hasan recited "al-Injīl" with a fatḥa on the hamza (al-Injīl), and this is easier than the case of al-Burṭīl (a Greek-derived word). Those who recited "al-sakīnah" and "al-ruʾbān" with a fatḥa on the fāʾ (al-sakīnah) did so because the word is non-Arabic, so there is no obligation to preserve the Arabic patterns (abniyah) in it. It was also recited as "ra'āfah" on the pattern "fa'ālah", meaning: We enabled them to show mercy and compassion toward one another. A similar description appears regarding the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "compassionate among themselves" (Qur'an 48:29).

"Monasticism" (al-rahbāniyyah): they became monks in the mountains, fleeing from tribulation in their religion, dedicating themselves to worship. This is because the tyrants (al-jabābirah) overpowered the believers after the death of Jesus, fought them three times, and killed them until only a few remained. They feared they would be tested in their religion, so they chose monasticism. Its meaning is the act attributed to the monks (al-ruhbān). [[Maḥmūd said: "al-Rahbāniyyah: the act attributed to the monks... etc." Aḥmad said: There is a problem here, for attributing to a plural in its own form is not accepted by them unless it is traced back to its singular, except that it may be said: when al-ruhbān became a specific group, this name, though a plural, became like a proper name for them, so it was joined with Anṣārī, Madā'inī, and Aʿrābī.]]

"Rahbān" means one who fears: fa'lān from rahiba, like khashyān from khashiya. It was also recited as "wa-rahbāniyyatan" with a ḍammah, as though it were a nisbah to al-rahbān, which is the plural of rāhib, like rākib and rukbān. Its accusative case is governed by a suppressed verb. [[Maḥmūd said: "It is in the accusative governed by a suppressed verb... etc." Aḥmad said: In the grammatical analysis of this verse, Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī became entangled, withdrew into the group of tribulation and the faction of innovation. He parsed "rahbāniyyah" as accusative governed by a suppressed verb that the apparent verb explains, and he justified the impossibility of coordination by saying: Do you not see that "rahbāniyyah" cannot be taken as the object of "jaʿalnā" together with its description by His words "ibtadaʿūhā," because what He makes (ja'ala) is not what they innovate (ibtada'ū)? Al-Zamakhsharī also took the same unworthy course, and his devil delivered him to the accursed one. So when he permitted what Abū ʿAlī forbade, namely making it coordinated, he excused it by altering "jaʿl" to "tawfīq" (granting success), fleeing from what Abū ʿAlī fled from: the belief that this is created by God Most High, and inclining toward association and the belief that what they do is not done or created by God Most High. Sufficient in this verse, beyond the decisive proofs and rational demonstrations, is evidence against the falsehood of what they believed: He mentioned the locus of mercy and compassion while knowing that its locus is the heart, so His words "in the hearts of those who followed him" were made an emphasis of His creating these meanings and a depiction of the meaning of creation by mentioning its locus. Had the intended meaning been something not created by God in their hearts, as they claimed, then His words "in the hearts of those who followed him" would have no place, and God is too exalted for His noble Book to contain what has no purpose. May God grant us the proof and guide us along the clear path; He is the Guardian of success and the Giver of verification.]]

Its interpretation is its estimated form: "And they innovated monasticism" (ibtadaʿūhā), meaning: they invented it themselves and vowed it. "We did not prescribe it for them" means we did not impose it on them, "except to seek the pleasure of God" (illā ibtighāʾa riḍwāni-llāh), an exceptive clause of disconnection, meaning: "But they innovated it seeking God's pleasure." "But they did not observe it with its due observance," as one who makes a vow is obligated to observe it, because it is a covenant with God that may not be broken. "So We gave those who believed," meaning the people of mercy and compassion who followed Jesus, "their reward, but many of them are defiantes," those who did not safeguard their vow.

It is permissible that "rahbāniyyah" be coordinated with what precedes it, and "ibtadaʿūhā" is a description of it in the accusative position, meaning: "And We placed in their hearts compassion and mercy and monasticism innovated by them," meaning: We enabled them to show mercy among themselves and to innovate and originate monasticism. "We did not prescribe it for them except that they might seek by it God's pleasure and deserve by it reward," on the basis that He prescribed it for them and obligated it upon them so that they might be freed from tribulations and seek by that God's pleasure and His reward. "But they did not all observe it with due observance; rather, some of them did. So We gave those among them who believed and observed monasticism their reward, but many of them are defiantes." These are the ones who did not observe it.

O you who believe! It is possible that this is an address to those among the People of the Book who believe, and "those who believe" (the phrase "wa-alladhina amanu" — possibly intended as "wa-alladhina amanu" with a correction noted by the editor, "(ʿ)") refers to others than them. If it is an address to the believers among the People of the Book, then the meaning is: O you who believe in Musa and Isa, believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), and He will give you a double portion (kiflayn) of His mercy, meaning two shares, for your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and your belief in those before him. And He will make for you on the Day of Resurrection a light by which you walk, which is the light mentioned in His words, "their light running before them." And He will forgive you what you had committed of disbelief and sins.

(li-allā yaʿlama) So that the People of the Book who have not embraced Islam may know—"lā" is extra (zāʾida). Allā yaqdirūna (that they do not have power) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "anna," originally: annahu lā yaqdirūna, meaning: the matter is that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah, i.e., they gain nothing of the bounty mentioned, namely the two portions of reward, the light, and the forgiveness, because they did not believe in the Messenger of Allah; so their faith in those before him did not benefit them, and it never earned them any merit.

And if the address is to others, then the meaning is: "Fear Allah, and remain steadfast in your faith in the Messenger of Allah, and He will give you what He promised to those of the People of the Book who believed, the two portions, in His saying: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾, and He will not diminish from you anything of the like of their reward, for you are like them in the two faiths, and you do not differentiate between any of His messengers."

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him) with seventy riders to the Negus, inviting him. Ja'far arrived and invited him, and he responded. Some people from among those of his kingdom who had believed, and they were forty men, said: "Permit us to travel to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He permitted them, and they came with Ja'far, while preparations for the Battle of Uhud were underway. When they saw the poverty among the Muslims, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission, and they returned and came back with their wealth, with which they assisted the Muslims. [[It is well known that Ja'far came after Uhud by some time; he came at the conquest of Khaybar.]]

Then Allah revealed: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book... ﴾ up to His saying ﴿...and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. When those among the People of the Book who had not believed heard His saying ﴿those will be given their reward twice﴾, they boasted over the Muslims and said: "As for one who believes in your Book and our Book, he has his reward twice, and as for one who does not believe in your Book, he has a reward like your reward; so what is your superiority over us?" Then it was revealed. It is also narrated that believing People of the Book boasted over other believers that they would be given their reward twice, and claimed superiority over them, so it was revealed.

It was recited as: li-kay yaʿlama; li-kayla yaʿlama; liyaʿlama; la-ann yaʿlama, with the nūn assimilated into the yāʾ. And li-yan yaʿlama, with the hamza changed to a yāʾ and the nūn assimilated into the yāʾ. From al-Ḥasan: laylā yaʿlama, with a fatḥa on the lām and a sukūn on the yāʾ. Qaṭrub narrated it with a kasra on the lām. It was said regarding its explanation: the hamza of anna was elided, and its nūn was assimilated into the lām of lā, so it became "lalā," then the assimilated lām was changed to a yāʾ, like their saying dīwān and qīrāṭ. As for one who vocalized the lām with a fatḥa, it is based on the fact that the original vowel of the prepositional lām is fatḥa, as the poet recited:

*Urīdu li-ansā dhikrahā* (I wish to forget her memory)... [[*Urīdu li-ansā dhikrahā fa-kaʾannamā ... tamaththala lī Laylā bi-kulli sabīl*: this is by Qays ibn al-Mulawwaḥ, the Majnūn of Layla al-ʿĀmiriyya. It was also said to be by Kuthayyir, the companion of ʿAzza, and he alluded to her by Layla as a veil. It was also said that Kuthayyir stole it from the poetry of Jamīl, the companion of Buthayna. His saying *li-ansā* with a fatḥa on the prepositional lām is according to the original in single particles, and that is the dialect of ʿUkl; it is necessarily so when it enters a verb in the subjunctive governed by an implied *anna*, as here. It is also reported with a kasra, according to the well-known dialect, meaning: "I wish for the forgetting of her remembrance"; the lām is extra, but it is what indicated the elision of *inna*. *Tamaththala*: its origin is *tatamaththalu*, meaning: Layla takes form and appears before me in every way, either sensorily or by way of remembrance, and the first is more apt, as evidenced by his saying *kaʾannamā*; and her appearance to him necessitates her remembrance. *Mā* is extra after *kāna*, restraining it from governing, which is why it entered upon the verb.]] ...

It was also recited: an lā yaqdirū bi-yadi Allāh, meaning in His dominion and His disposal. "Yad" (hand) is like His saying ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, and He wills only to give to one who deserves it. From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, he will be recorded among those who believe in Allah and His messengers."
